title: KV cache concurrent-write thrash causing TTL staleness and memory amplification
creator: Alex Kim
description: Summary: During a peak capacity event on 2026-02-17 we observed cascading latency spikes and memory growth originating from the KV prefix cache. Symptoms included frequent and concurrent write storms to the same prefix buckets, TTLs not expiring as expected (stale entries persisted), and eviction machinery oscillating which amplified memory pressure and caused degraded serving performance. This ticket captures the investigation, short-term mitigations, and a prioritized set of long-term fixes.
incident_timeline:
2026-02-17 03:12 UTC - Pager alert: host pool for region-us-east-1 reported OOM kills and 99th percentile tail latency > 2x SLA.
2026-02-17 03:18 UTC - Ops initiated autoscaling and started query reroutes; initial mitigation reduced client 5xxs but tail latency persisted.
2026-02-17 03:35 UTC - Engineering confirmed KV cache slab growth and eviction thrash on multiple nodes; observed heavy write contention to prefix buckets from a batch job rollout.
2026-02-17 04:10 UTC - Temporary mitigations applied: rate limit the background batch job, enable conservative eviction backoff, and increase soft memory headroom on affected nodes.
2026-02-17 08:00 UTC - Service recovered to acceptable SLOs; incident declared mitigated.
2026-02-18 - Post-incident analysis started; memory heap dump and trace captures uploaded for deeper analysis.
root_cause_summary: Multiple contributing factors: (1) a recent internal rollout (job-engine v3.9) introduced a background sstable compaction-style task that aggressively refreshed keys in the prefix cache, causing high concurrent writes to the same prefix namespace; (2) the TTL eviction path assumed monotonic increments and missed a race where writes reset TTLs while eviction scans were in-flight, leading to stale entries surviving; (3) eviction scoring used a decay window that overreacted to oscillating write metrics, causing eviction storms instead of graceful degradation; (4) insufficient telemetry meant we didn't catch the pattern earlier. The combined interactions produced memory amplification and increased GC time which impacted latency SLOs.
mitigations_deployed: Hotfix v1: throttled internal background job (job-engine v3.9) to max 5 concurrent writers per prefix namespace
Hotfix v2: flip on conservative eviction-backoff flag to prevent immediate re-eviction after insert
Hotfix v3: increased soft memory limit on affected node pool to reduce OOM flapping during cleanup
Monitoring: added immediate alert rule for per-prefix concurrent write rate and eviction oscillation ratio
long_term_actions: Redesign prefix write path to use per-prefix write coalescing (owner: Priya Nair) - reduces duplicate writes under rollout churn
Fix TTL race: ensure eviction scanner uses a stable snapshot of last-write timestamps or compare-and-evict semantics (owner: Marco Alvarez)
Revise eviction scoring: implement hysteresis and dampening to avoid oscillation (owner: Samira Zhou)
Instrumentation: emit per-prefix cardinality, write hotness, and KV slab fragmentation metrics to allow early detection (owner: Alex Kim)
Stress tests: add e2e rollout simulation that exercises concurrent background refreshers against realistic traffic patterns (owner: QA team)
Capacity guardrails: implement autoscaler cooldown tied to cache reclamation progress (owner: Infra)
Audit: code review of all background jobs that touch KV cache to add safety limits and idempotency guarantees (owner: Eng Leads)

progress_updates:
2026-02-19: Heap trace indicates repeated allocation peaks tied to KV slab reallocations.
2026-02-22: Prototype coalescer reduces write amplification by ~7x in synthetic harness.
2026-02-25: Dashboard live; alert triggered once during rollout rehearsal.

notes:
Trade-offs discussed: coalescing reduces parallelism on hot prefixes which could increase latency for some write paths; proposed approach is to limit coalescing to background/maintenance jobs and keep foreground writes low-latency. We debated changing eviction aggressiveness versus improving write-side correctness; team prioritized correctness first.
Open question: whether to expose per-namespace write throttles as a runtime config for large enterprise customers. Defer to product discussion after safety improvements.
final_notes: This ticket is the canonical follow-up for the 2026-02-17 KV prefix cache thrash. The short-term mitigations have stabilized customer impact; long-term fixes are prioritized into runtime-1.26. Revisit after post-change run for at least 2 weeks of normal workload to consider the ticket for Done.
